tool.name: Ollama
tool.tagline: Run open LLMs on your own computer or server, with a CLI, desktop app and local API
tool.description: Ollama downloads and runs open-weight language models (such as Gemma, Llama, Qwen and gpt-oss) on your own Mac, Windows or Linux machine. It offers a desktop app, a command-line tool, a local REST API with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and official Python and JavaScript libraries, so apps and frameworks can use local models for chat, embeddings, tool calling and structured output. Optional cloud models run larger models on Ollama's servers through the same interface.

concepts.name: What Ollama is
concepts.summary: Understand what it means to run a language model locally and what Ollama gives you to do it.
concepts.why: Running models yourself changes the trade-offs on privacy, cost and quality, so it helps to know what you are getting.
concepts.body:
When you use ChatGPT or Claude in a browser, the model runs on the company's computers. Your text travels over the internet, and you pay per use or by subscription.

Some language models are **open-weight**: their creators publish the trained model files (the "weights", billions of numbers learned during training), so anyone can download and run them. Examples include Google's Gemma, Meta's Llama, Alibaba's Qwen and OpenAI's gpt-oss.

**Ollama** is a free program that makes running those models on your own computer easy. It:

- downloads models from its online library with one command,
- runs them using your graphics card (GPU) when possible, or your processor (CPU),
- gives you a chat in the terminal and a desktop app,
- runs a small local **server** (a program that waits for requests) so your own code and other apps can use the models through an API on your machine.

Why people use it:

- **Privacy**: prompts and documents stay on your machine.
- **No per-request cost**: once downloaded, using a model is free (apart from electricity and hardware).
- **Offline use**: works without internet.
- **Experimenting**: try many open models quickly.

The trade-off: models small enough for a laptop are usually less capable than the biggest hosted models, and speed depends on your hardware. Ollama also offers optional **cloud models**, which run bigger models on Ollama's servers through the same commands; a later lesson covers when that makes sense.
takeaways: Open-weight models can be downloaded and run by anyone
Ollama downloads, runs and serves them locally via CLI, app and API
Local = private, offline and free per use, but limited by your hardware
pitfalls: Expecting a small laptop model to match the quality of the largest hosted models on hard reasoning tasks.

quiz.q: What does Ollama's local server let you do?
options: Let your own programs and other apps use local models through an API
Share your GPU over the internet automatically
quiz.explain: The server listens for API requests on your machine, so code and tools can call the models.

concepts.name: Installing Ollama
concepts.summary: Install Ollama on macOS, Windows or Linux, and check that the app and background server are running.
concepts.why: Every other lesson assumes a working install with the server listening on its default port.
concepts.body:
Download Ollama from the official site, ollama.com/download.

- **macOS and Windows**: install the desktop app like any other program. It starts the Ollama server in the background and shows an icon in the menu bar or system tray. The app also includes a chat window and settings.
- **Linux**: run the official install script in a terminal: `curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh`. It installs the `ollama` command and sets it up as a background service (on most distributions with systemd, the system that starts services at boot).

Either way you get the **`ollama` command** for the terminal and a **server** listening on your machine at `http://localhost:11434`. "localhost" means "this computer", and 11434 is the port, a numbered door that programs use to reach the server.

Check it works:

```bash
ollama --version
curl http://localhost:11434
```

The second command should reply "Ollama is running". If it doesn't, start the app (macOS, Windows) or run `ollama serve` in a terminal (Linux, when the service isn't running).

Updating: macOS and Windows download updates automatically and ask you to restart. On Linux, run the install script again.

Downloaded models are large (often several gigabytes each) and stored in your home folder by default (`~/.ollama/models` on macOS and Windows). Make sure you have disk space; a later lesson shows how to move them.
concepts.code:
# macOS / Windows: install the app from https://ollama.com/download
# Linux:
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

ollama --version                 # ollama version is 0.40.x
curl http://localhost:11434      # Ollama is running

# If the server is not running (e.g. Linux without the service):
ollama serve
takeaways: App on macOS/Windows, install script on Linux
The server listens on http://localhost:11434
`ollama --version` and `curl localhost:11434` confirm it works
pitfalls: Running `ollama serve` while the app or service is already running, which fails because the port is already in use.

quiz.q: What does http://localhost:11434 refer to?
options: The Ollama server running on your own computer
quiz.explain: localhost means this machine; 11434 is the port the local Ollama server listens on.

concepts.name: Chatting with ollama run
concepts.summary: Download and chat with a model in the terminal using ollama run, one-shot prompts and in-chat commands.
concepts.why: The terminal chat is the fastest way to try a model and check that everything works.
concepts.body:
To chat with a model:

```bash
ollama run gemma4:e2b
```

The first time, Ollama downloads the model (several gigabytes), then opens an interactive chat with a `>>>` prompt. Type a message and press Enter. Model names in this course come from the official docs and will change over time; browse ollama.com/library for current ones.

Useful things inside the chat (type them at the `>>>` prompt):

- `/bye` leaves the chat.
- `/clear` forgets the conversation so far.
- `/set system You are a concise assistant.` sets a system prompt.
- `/set parameter temperature 0.2` changes a setting for this session.
- `/show info` shows details about the model.
- `/?` lists all commands.
- Wrap text in `"""` to type several lines.

**One-shot prompts** run a single question and exit, which is handy in scripts:

```bash
ollama run gemma4:e2b "Summarize what a Linux kernel is in one sentence."
```

You can also pipe a file in: `cat notes.txt | ollama run gemma4:e2b "Summarize this:"`. For models that understand images, include an image file path in the prompt.

Flags worth knowing: `--verbose` prints speed statistics (tokens per second) after each answer, and `--think` turns on thinking mode for models that support it.

The desktop app on macOS and Windows offers the same chats in a window, with a model picker.
concepts.code:
ollama run gemma4:e2b                       # downloads once, then opens a chat
>>> /set system You answer in one short sentence.
>>> Why is the sky blue?
Sunlight scatters off air molecules, and blue light scatters the most.
>>> /bye

# One-shot prompt (prints the answer and exits)
ollama run gemma4:e2b "Give me three names for a cat."

# Pipe a file in, and show speed statistics
cat meeting.txt | ollama run gemma4:e2b --verbose "List the action items:"
# ... eval rate: 38.5 tokens/s
takeaways: `ollama run MODEL` downloads if needed and opens a chat
In-chat: `/bye`, `/clear`, `/set system`, `/set parameter`, `/?`
`ollama run MODEL "prompt"` for one-shot use; `--verbose` shows speed
pitfalls: Assuming a model remembers earlier sessions; each new `ollama run` starts with an empty conversation.

quiz.q: You want to test a model quickly from a shell script without an interactive chat. What do you use?
quiz.explain: Passing the prompt as an argument runs one answer and exits.

concepts.name: Managing downloaded models
concepts.summary: Download, list, inspect, stop, copy and delete models with pull, ls, ps, show, stop, cp and rm.
concepts.why: Models take gigabytes of disk and memory, so you need to know what is installed and what is loaded.
concepts.body:
Ollama keeps models on disk and loads them into memory when used. The main commands:

- `ollama pull gemma4:e2b` downloads (or updates) a model without starting a chat.
- `ollama ls` (or `ollama list`) shows downloaded models with their size and when they were changed.
- `ollama ps` shows models currently **loaded in memory**, how much memory they use, whether they run on GPU or CPU, the context size, and when they will be unloaded.
- `ollama stop gemma4:e2b` unloads a model from memory now (it stays on disk).
- `ollama show gemma4:e2b` prints details: parameter count, quantization, context length and capabilities such as tools or vision. `--modelfile` shows its recipe (a later lesson).
- `ollama cp gemma4:e2b my-gemma` makes a copy under a new name.
- `ollama rm gemma4:e2b` deletes it from disk.

**Names and tags.** A model name has a family and a **tag** after the colon: `qwen3:8b`, `gemma4:e2b`. Tags usually mark the size or variant. Without a tag, Ollama uses `latest`, which is the family's default variant. Pin a specific tag in scripts and apps so they don't change unexpectedly when the default moves.

Loaded models stay in memory for a while after the last request (5 minutes by default), so the next request is fast. That is why `ollama ps` can show models you're not actively using.

Running `ollama pull` again on an existing model downloads only the changed parts, so it is the way to update a model.
concepts.code:
ollama pull qwen3:8b            # download without running
ollama ls
# NAME          ID              SIZE      MODIFIED
# qwen3:8b      500a1f067a9f    5.2 GB    2 minutes ago
# gemma4:e2b    7c1fa3e5a1b2    7.2 GB    3 days ago

ollama ps                       # what is loaded right now
# NAME        ID       SIZE    PROCESSOR    CONTEXT   UNTIL
# qwen3:8b    500a...  6.9 GB  100% GPU     4096      4 minutes from now

ollama show qwen3:8b            # parameters, quantization, context, capabilities
ollama stop qwen3:8b            # free the memory now
ollama rm gemma4:e2b            # delete from disk
takeaways: `pull`, `ls`, `rm` manage models on disk
`ps` and `stop` manage models loaded in memory
Names are family:tag; pin tags in apps instead of relying on `latest`
pitfalls: Deleting a model with rm when you only wanted to free memory; use ollama stop for that.

quiz.q: Which command tells you whether a loaded model is running on the GPU or the CPU?
quiz.explain: ollama ps lists loaded models with a PROCESSOR column such as 100% GPU or a CPU/GPU split.

concepts.name: Choosing a model
concepts.summary: Pick a model family and size for your task by reading the library: parameters, capabilities and context length.
concepts.why: The right model is the difference between a fast, useful assistant and a slow or useless one.
concepts.body:
The Ollama library (ollama.com/library and ollama.com/search) lists models with their sizes and **capabilities**. Choosing comes down to three questions.

**1. What must it do?** Look for capability tags:

- **tools**: can request function calls, needed for agents.
- **vision**: understands images.
- **thinking**: can reason step by step before answering.
- **embedding**: produces vectors for search, not chat.

**2. How big can it be?** Size is measured in **parameters**, the learned numbers inside the model, written like `8b` (8 billion). As a rough guide:

- 1 to 4 billion: fast on almost any machine; fine for simple rewriting, classification and extraction.
- 7 to 14 billion: good general assistants on a decent laptop or a single gaming GPU.
- 20 to 35 billion: noticeably smarter; needs a lot of memory.
- 70 billion and up: workstation or server territory.

Some models use a **mixture of experts** design: they contain many parameters but use only part of them for each word, so they run faster than their total size suggests.

**3. How much text must it handle?** The context length you need (long documents, agents) costs memory too (a later lesson).

Practical approach: start with a well-known, recent family in a size your hardware handles, test it on 10 to 20 real examples from your task, then try one size up and one size down. Specialised variants (for code, or instruction-tuned versions) often beat larger general ones on their speciality.

Leaderboards are a starting point, not an answer; your own examples decide.
concepts.code:
# See what a model can do before relying on it
ollama show qwen3:8b               # (example output; details vary by version)
#   Model
#     architecture        qwen3
#     parameters          8.2B
#     context length      40960
#     quantization        Q4_K_M
#   Capabilities
#     completion
#     tools
#     thinking

# Compare two sizes on the same real task
ollama run qwen3:4b "Classify as billing/bug/other: 'I was charged twice.'"
ollama run qwen3:8b "Classify as billing/bug/other: 'I was charged twice.'"
takeaways: Match capabilities (tools, vision, thinking, embedding) to the task
Parameters (e.g. 8b) drive quality, speed and memory
Test candidates on your own examples, one size up and down
pitfalls: Picking the biggest model that barely fits, which then runs partly on the CPU and is too slow to use.

quiz.q: You need a local model for an agent that calls functions. What should you check first in the library?
options: That it has the tools capability
That it is the largest available
That it is an embedding model
quiz.explain: Only models trained for tool calling can request function calls reliably.

concepts.name: Memory, GPUs and quantization
concepts.summary: Estimate whether a model fits your RAM or GPU memory, and understand quantization in simple terms.
concepts.why: Fitting the model in fast memory decides whether you get a few words per second or dozens.
concepts.body:
A model must be loaded into memory to run. Where it fits decides the speed:

- **GPU memory (VRAM)**: the graphics card's own memory. Fastest.
- **Unified memory** on Apple Silicon Macs: shared by CPU and GPU, also fast. A 16 GB Mac can use most, but not all, of it for models.
- **Normal RAM with the CPU**: works, but often 5 to 20 times slower.

If a model doesn't fit in VRAM, Ollama splits it between GPU and CPU. `ollama ps` shows this, for example `48%/52% CPU/GPU`. A split usually means a big slowdown.

**Quantization** is how big models fit at all. Each parameter is a number. Stored at full precision it takes 2 bytes. Quantization stores it with fewer bits, like saving a photo as a smaller JPEG: a little detail is lost, but the file shrinks a lot.

- 16-bit: original quality, 2 bytes per parameter.
- 8-bit (Q8): about 1 byte, nearly no quality loss.
- 4-bit (Q4, such as `Q4_K_M`): about 0.5 to 0.6 bytes, a small loss; the usual default in the Ollama library.

A rough rule: **model size ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter**, plus room for the context. An 8 billion parameter model at 4-bit is about 5 GB, so it fits a GPU with 8 GB. The same model at 16-bit needs about 16 GB. `ollama ls` shows real sizes.

Ollama supports NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs (through ROCm), Apple's Metal, and other GPUs through Vulkan. Without a supported GPU it uses the CPU.

Rule of thumb: a smaller model fully on the GPU usually beats a bigger one split onto the CPU.
concepts.code:
# Rough memory estimate for model weights (context needs extra memory on top)
def weights_gb(billion_params: float, bits: int) -> float:
    return billion_params * bits / 8          # 1e9 params * bits/8 bytes = GB

for name, b in [("4B", 4), ("8B", 8), ("27B", 27)]:
    print(name, f"4-bit ~{weights_gb(b, 4):.0f} GB,", f"8-bit ~{weights_gb(b, 8):.0f} GB,",
          f"16-bit ~{weights_gb(b, 16):.0f} GB")
# 4B 4-bit ~2 GB, 8-bit ~4 GB, 16-bit ~8 GB
# 8B 4-bit ~4 GB, 8-bit ~8 GB, 16-bit ~16 GB
# 27B 4-bit ~14 GB, 8-bit ~27 GB, 16-bit ~54 GB
# (real 4-bit files are a bit larger, e.g. ~5 GB for 8B, because some layers keep more bits)
takeaways: Fastest when the whole model fits in GPU or unified memory
Quantization stores parameters with fewer bits; 4-bit is the common default
Size ≈ parameters × bits / 8, plus memory for context
pitfalls: Ignoring a CPU/GPU split in `ollama ps` and blaming the model for being slow.

quiz.q: Roughly how much memory do the weights of a 14-billion-parameter model need at 4-bit quantization?
quiz.explain: 14 billion × 4 bits / 8 ≈ 7 GB, plus a bit extra for layers kept at higher precision.

concepts.name: Context length in Ollama
concepts.summary: Know Ollama's default context length, how to raise it in the app, server, chat and API, and what it costs in memory.
concepts.why: Too small a context silently cuts off long documents and agent conversations; too large wastes memory.
concepts.body:
The context window is how much text (in tokens) a model can consider at once: your prompt, the conversation so far and its answer. A model *supports* some maximum (shown by `ollama show`), but Ollama decides how much to *allocate* when loading it, because every extra token of context needs memory.

**Default.** Ollama picks a default based on your GPU memory: 4,096 tokens with less than 24 GB, 32,768 with 24 to 48 GB, and 262,144 (256k) with 48 GB or more. Cloud models use their maximum.

That 4k default on ordinary machines is small: roughly 3,000 words in total. If your prompt is longer, the oldest part is dropped and the model never sees it, usually without an error. Agents, coding tools and document questions need much more; the docs suggest at least 64,000 tokens for agents and coding tools.

**Changing it:**

- Desktop app: the context length slider in Settings.
- Server-wide: start the server with the environment variable `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768`.
- In a chat: `/set parameter num_ctx 32768`.
- Per API request: `"options": {"num_ctx": 32768}`.
- In a custom model: `PARAMETER num_ctx 32768` in a Modelfile.

**Checking it:** `ollama ps` shows the allocated context in the CONTEXT column, next to the CPU/GPU split.

Memory grows with context. If raising it pushes part of the model onto the CPU, speed drops sharply. Find the largest context that still keeps the model 100% on the GPU, or pick a smaller model.
concepts.code:
# Server-wide default (Linux/macOS shell; restart the server after changing it)
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 ollama serve

# Per chat session
ollama run qwen3:8b
>>> /set parameter num_ctx 32768

# Per API request
curl http://localhost:11434/api/chat -d '{
  "model": "qwen3:8b",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this long report: ..."}],
  "options": {"num_ctx": 32768},
  "stream": false
}'

ollama ps     # CONTEXT column shows 32768; check PROCESSOR is still 100% GPU
takeaways: Default context depends on VRAM: 4k under 24 GB, then 32k, then 256k
Raise it with the app slider, OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH, num_ctx or a Modelfile
More context needs more memory; keep the model fully on the GPU
pitfalls: Sending a 20-page document with the default 4k context and trusting the summary, although most of the document was cut off.

quiz.q: A summary of a long document ignores everything except the last few pages. What is the likely cause?
options: The context length is too small, so earlier text was dropped
quiz.explain: Text beyond the allocated context is truncated, so the model only saw the end.

concepts.name: When local beats hosted, and when not
concepts.summary: Decide between local Ollama models and hosted APIs based on privacy, cost, quality, speed and operations.
concepts.why: Choosing the wrong side wastes money, time or quality; many teams end up using both.
concepts.body:
Local and hosted models each win in different situations.

**Local (Ollama on your own hardware) is a good fit when:**

- Data is sensitive: health, legal or customer data that may not leave your network.
- You need offline use, for example on a plane, in a lab or on a factory floor.
- Volume is high and tasks are simple (classifying or extracting from thousands of documents), where per-request fees add up.
- You want predictable behaviour: a model file you control doesn't change unless you update it.
- You are learning and experimenting.

**Hosted APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and others) are a better fit when:**

- You need the strongest reasoning, writing or coding quality available; the largest models don't fit on ordinary hardware.
- You have spiky or low volume, so paying per request is cheaper than buying GPUs.
- Many users need fast answers at once; providers have far more hardware.
- You don't want to operate servers, GPUs and updates.

**Hidden costs of local:** hardware, electricity, your time for setup and updates, and slower speed on modest machines. **Hidden costs of hosted:** data agreements, rate limits, price changes and model retirements.

**Common hybrid pattern:** develop and test locally, run private or bulk tasks on local models, and send the hard minority of tasks to a hosted model. Ollama's OpenAI-compatible API (a later lesson) makes switching mostly a configuration change. Ollama's own cloud models are a middle ground: bigger open models through the same tool, but your data then leaves your machine.

Decide with a small test: run your real examples through both and compare quality, speed and cost.
takeaways: Local wins on privacy, offline use, high-volume simple tasks and control
Hosted wins on top quality, bursty demand and zero operations
Hybrid setups are common; compare on your own examples
pitfalls: Comparing only per-request prices while ignoring hardware, electricity and maintenance time for local setups.

quiz.q: A hospital wants to summarise patient notes, which must not leave its network. What fits best?
options: A hosted API with a free plan
A local model served with Ollama inside the network
quiz.explain: Local models keep data on the hospital's own machines, which is the key requirement here.

concepts.name: The local REST API
concepts.summary: Call Ollama's HTTP API with /api/chat and /api/generate, handle streaming responses, and list models over HTTP.
concepts.why: Every app, library and integration talks to Ollama through this API, so knowing it makes debugging easy.
concepts.body:
The Ollama server answers HTTP requests at `http://localhost:11434`. Any language that can send HTTP requests can use it. The main endpoints:

- `POST /api/chat`: send a list of `messages` (each with a `role` of `system`, `user`, `assistant` or `tool`, and `content`), get the next assistant message. Used for conversations and most apps.
- `POST /api/generate`: send a single `prompt` string, get a completion. Simpler; good for one-off tasks.
- `POST /api/embed`: turn text into embedding vectors.
- `GET /api/tags`: list downloaded models. `GET /api/ps`: list loaded models.
- `POST /api/pull`, `POST /api/show`, `DELETE /api/delete`: manage models.

**Streaming is on by default.** The reply arrives as many small JSON objects, one per line (a format called NDJSON). Each contains a piece of text in `message.content`; the last one has `"done": true` plus statistics such as `eval_count` (tokens generated) and durations in nanoseconds. Set `"stream": false` to receive a single JSON object instead.

Other common request fields:

- `options`: model settings such as `temperature`, `num_ctx`, `seed`, `num_predict` (a later lesson).
- `format`: `"json"` or a JSON schema for structured output.
- `tools`: functions the model may call.
- `keep_alive`: how long to keep the model loaded afterwards.

The API is **stateless**: it doesn't remember earlier requests. To continue a conversation, send the whole message history each time.

Errors come back as an HTTP error status with an `error` message, for example when a model name isn't downloaded.
takeaways: `/api/chat` takes messages; `/api/generate` takes a prompt
Streaming NDJSON is the default; `"stream": false` returns one object
Stateless: resend the conversation history on every call
pitfalls: Parsing a streaming response as a single JSON document, which fails because it is many JSON lines.

quiz.q: Your code calls /api/chat without setting stream and json.loads(response_text) fails. Why?
options: The response is streamed as many JSON lines by default
quiz.explain: Streaming is on by default; set stream to false or parse line by line.

concepts.name: The official Python library
concepts.summary: Use the ollama Python package to chat, stream, set options and connect to remote servers with Client.
concepts.why: The library wraps the REST API with typed responses and less code, and is the quickest path from Python.
concepts.body:
Install the official library with `pip install ollama`. It talks to the local server for you.

**Chat:**

```python
from ollama import chat
response = chat(model="gemma4:e2b", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi!"}])
print(response.message.content)
```

The `messages` list holds dictionaries with `role` and `content`, exactly like the REST API. The response is an object: `response.message.content` is the text, and fields like `response.eval_count` hold statistics. (Dictionary-style access such as `response["message"]["content"]` also works.)

**Streaming:** pass `stream=True` and loop over the result; each chunk has a piece of text in `chunk.message.content`.

**Settings:** `options={"temperature": 0, "num_ctx": 8192}` sets model parameters; `keep_alive="10m"` controls how long the model stays loaded.

**Other functions** mirror the API: `generate(model, prompt)`, `embed(model, input)`, `list()`, `ps()`, `pull(model)`, `show(model)`, `delete(model)`.

**Another machine:** create a `Client(host="http://192.168.1.50:11434")` and call the same methods on it (`client.chat(...)`). The `OLLAMA_HOST` environment variable also changes the default address.

**Async code:** `AsyncClient` offers the same methods for programs that handle many requests at once.

Errors raise `ollama.ResponseError`, which has `.status_code` and `.error`. A common one is 404 when the model isn't downloaded; you can catch it and call `pull` automatically.

Remember the API is stateless: append each reply to your `messages` list to keep a conversation going.
concepts.code:
# pip install ollama
import ollama
from ollama import Client, chat

messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise assistant."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "Name two uses of a hash map."}]

reply = chat(model="gemma4:e2b", messages=messages, options={"temperature": 0})
print(reply.message.content)          # Caching lookups and counting items.
messages.append(reply.message)        # keep the conversation going

for chunk in chat(model="gemma4:e2b", stream=True,
                  messages=messages + [{"role": "user", "content": "One more?"}]):
    print(chunk.message.content, end="", flush=True)

try:
    chat(model="not-downloaded:1b", messages=messages)
except ollama.ResponseError as e:
    print("\nError:", e.status_code, e.error)    # Error: 404 model 'not-downloaded:1b' not found

remote = Client(host="http://192.168.1.50:11434")  # a server elsewhere on your network
takeaways: `chat(model, messages)` returns `response.message.content`
`stream=True`, `options={...}` and `keep_alive` mirror the API
`Client(host=...)` for other servers; `AsyncClient` for async code
pitfalls: Forgetting to append the assistant's reply to messages, so the model loses track of the conversation.

quiz.q: How do you use the Python library against Ollama running on another machine?
quiz.explain: Client takes a host URL; the server there must be configured to accept network connections.

concepts.name: OpenAI-compatible endpoint
concepts.summary: Point OpenAI client libraries and tools at Ollama's /v1 endpoint to switch between hosted and local models.
concepts.why: Many apps and libraries only speak the OpenAI API; compatibility lets them use local models unchanged.
concepts.body:
Many tools and libraries were written for OpenAI's API. Ollama also offers an **OpenAI-compatible API** under `http://localhost:11434/v1/`, so you can point that code at Ollama by changing two settings:

- `base_url` (the server address) to `http://localhost:11434/v1/`,
- `api_key` to any non-empty string, such as `"ollama"`. It is required by the client library but ignored by a local server.

Supported endpoints include:

- `/v1/chat/completions`: chat, streaming, JSON mode and structured output, tools, and base64 images.
- `/v1/completions`: plain text completions.
- `/v1/embeddings`: embeddings.
- `/v1/models`: list models.
- `/v1/responses`: OpenAI's newer Responses API, without its stateful features (you send the full history yourself).

Limitations to know: some parameters aren't supported (for example `logprobs`, `tool_choice`, `n`), and images must be sent as base64 data rather than URLs. There is also no parameter for context length. To use a bigger context through this API, create a custom model with `PARAMETER num_ctx` in a Modelfile, or set `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH` on the server.

Ollama also has an Anthropic-compatible endpoint for tools that use Anthropic's Messages API, and the same `/v1` paths work against `https://ollama.com/v1` for cloud models with an API key.

Native `/api/...` endpoints expose more Ollama-specific options (`keep_alive`, `think`, every model option), so prefer them, or the `ollama` library, when you don't need OpenAI compatibility.
concepts.code:
# pip install openai
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1/", api_key="ollama")   # key is ignored locally

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-oss:20b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say this is a test"}],
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)          # This is a test.

emb = client.embeddings.create(model="embeddinggemma", input=["hello", "world"])
print(len(emb.data), len(emb.data[0].embedding))   # 2 768

print([m.id for m in client.models.list().data])   # ['gpt-oss:20b', 'embeddinggemma:latest', ...]
takeaways: Use `base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1/"` and a dummy `api_key`
Chat, completions, embeddings, models and (stateless) Responses are supported
No context-length parameter: use a Modelfile or OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH
pitfalls: Expecting num_ctx in an OpenAI-compatible request to change the context; set it via a Modelfile or the server instead.

quiz.q: An app only supports the OpenAI API. What do you change to make it use a local Ollama model?
options: Install the ollama Python library inside the app
Its base URL to http://localhost:11434/v1/, any API key, and the model name
quiz.explain: The /v1 endpoint speaks the OpenAI protocol, so only the address, key and model name change.

concepts.name: Modelfiles and custom models
concepts.summary: Write a Modelfile with FROM, PARAMETER, SYSTEM and MESSAGE, build it with ollama create, and inspect existing ones.
concepts.why: Custom models package a base model with your settings and instructions, so every app gets the same behaviour.
concepts.body:
A **Modelfile** is a small text file describing a model: which base model to use and which settings and instructions to add. It is like a recipe: the ingredients (weights) stay the same, but you fix the seasoning.

```
FROM qwen3:8b
PARAMETER temperature 0.2
PARAMETER num_ctx 16384
SYSTEM You are a support assistant for Acme. Answer in at most 3 sentences.
```

Build and use it:

```bash
ollama create acme-support -f Modelfile
ollama run acme-support
```

The new model shares the base model's weights on disk, so it takes almost no extra space.

Instructions (not case-sensitive, any order):

- `FROM` (required): the base model, or a path to model files (see the importing lesson).
- `PARAMETER name value`: default settings such as `temperature`, `num_ctx`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `repeat_penalty`, `seed`, `num_predict` and `stop`. Repeat `stop` for several stop sequences.
- `SYSTEM`: the system prompt. Use `"""` around multi-line text.
- `MESSAGE role content`: example conversation turns (`user`, `assistant`), a built-in few-shot example.
- `TEMPLATE`: the prompt format the model was trained with. Usually inherited from the base; rarely edit it.
- `LICENSE`: license text. `REQUIRES`: a minimum Ollama version.

Inspect any model's recipe with `ollama show qwen3:8b --modelfile`.

Settings sent in an API request override the Modelfile's defaults, so the Modelfile sets sensible defaults while apps can still adjust them. Keep Modelfiles in version control next to the code that uses them.
concepts.code:
# File: Modelfile
FROM qwen3:8b
PARAMETER temperature 0.2
PARAMETER num_ctx 16384
PARAMETER stop "<END>"
SYSTEM """You are Acme's support assistant.
Answer in at most 3 sentences. If unsure, say you will escalate."""
MESSAGE user Where is my order?
MESSAGE assistant I can check that. Please share your order number (it starts with A-).

# Terminal
ollama create acme-support -f Modelfile
ollama run acme-support "My parcel is late."
# I'm sorry about the delay. Please share your order number (it starts with A-) ...
ollama show acme-support --modelfile      # view the full recipe
takeaways: `FROM` + `PARAMETER` + `SYSTEM` (+ `MESSAGE`) define a custom model
`ollama create NAME -f Modelfile` builds it; it reuses the base weights
API request options override Modelfile defaults
pitfalls: Copying a TEMPLATE from another model family, which breaks the prompt format and produces garbled answers.

quiz.q: You build three custom models from the same 5 GB base model. How much extra disk space do they roughly use?
options: Almost none; they share the base weights
quiz.explain: Custom models reference the same weight files and only add small configuration layers.

concepts.name: Generation parameters
concepts.summary: Control randomness, length, stopping and reproducibility with temperature, top_p, num_predict, stop and seed.
concepts.why: The right settings make outputs consistent for automation and lively for creative tasks.
concepts.body:
Parameters change how the model picks each next token. You can set them in four places: `/set parameter` in a chat, `PARAMETER` in a Modelfile, the `options` field of an API request, or `options=` in the Python library. Request options override Modelfile defaults.

The ones you'll use most:

- `temperature`: randomness. Low values (0 to 0.3) give focused, repeatable answers for extraction, classification and code; higher values (0.7 to 1) give more variety for brainstorming and writing. Ollama's default is 0.8, but many models ship their own defaults.
- `top_p` and `top_k`: limit which tokens may be picked to the most likely ones. Change these rarely; adjust temperature first.
- `num_predict`: the maximum number of tokens to generate. The default -1 means no limit; set a limit to bound cost and time.
- `stop`: text sequences that end the answer immediately, such as `"\n\n"` or a closing tag.
- `seed`: with a fixed seed and the same prompt and settings, the output is usually repeatable, which helps testing.
- `repeat_penalty`: discourages repeating the same words; raise it slightly if a model loops.
- `num_ctx`: the context length (its own lesson).

Model creators tune defaults for their model, visible with `ollama show MODEL --parameters`. Start from those and change one setting at a time while testing on real examples.

Reasoning ("thinking") models often recommend specific settings in their model card. Follow them; very low temperatures can make some of these models repeat themselves.
concepts.code:
from ollama import chat

prompt = [{"role": "user", "content": "Invent a name for a coffee shop."}]

for t in (0.0, 1.0):
    names = [chat(model="gemma4:e2b", messages=prompt,
                  options={"temperature": t, "num_predict": 12}).message.content
             for _ in range(3)]
    print(t, names)
# 0.0 ['Bean There', 'Bean There', 'Bean There']        (same every time)
# 1.0 ['The Daily Grind', 'Brew Haven', 'Morning Ritual'] (varies)

fixed = {"temperature": 0.7, "seed": 42}
a = chat(model="gemma4:e2b", messages=prompt, options=fixed).message.content
b = chat(model="gemma4:e2b", messages=prompt, options=fixed).message.content
print(a == b)                                             # usually True: same seed, same output

short = chat(model="gemma4:e2b", messages=prompt, options={"stop": ["\n"]})
takeaways: Set options via chat, Modelfile, API `options` or `options=` in Python
Low temperature for automation, higher for creative work
`num_predict`, `stop` and `seed` bound length and aid reproducibility
pitfalls: Tuning top_p, top_k and temperature all at once, making it impossible to tell which change helped.

quiz.q: A script extracts invoice numbers and sometimes returns different results for the same input. What should you change first?
options: Lower temperature (e.g. to 0) and optionally fix the seed
quiz.explain: Low temperature and a fixed seed make outputs more deterministic, which suits extraction.

concepts.name: Embeddings with Ollama
concepts.summary: Create embeddings locally with embedding models and /api/embed, and use them for semantic search.
concepts.why: Local embeddings let you build private search and RAG without sending documents to anyone.
concepts.body:
Embedding models turn text into vectors (lists of numbers) so that texts with similar meaning have similar vectors. Ollama runs them locally like any other model; the docs use `embeddinggemma`, and the library has others such as `nomic-embed-text` and `mxbai-embed-large`.

Create embeddings with the Python library:

```python
import ollama
result = ollama.embed(model="embeddinggemma", input=["first text", "second text"])
vectors = result.embeddings      # a list of vectors, one per input
```

or with `POST /api/embed` and the same fields. Pass a list to embed many texts in one request, which is much faster than one call each.

Facts that matter:

- Vector length depends on the model, typically 384 to 1,024 numbers.
- `/api/embed` returns **normalised** vectors (length 1), so cosine similarity equals the plain dot product: multiply matching numbers and add them up.
- Use the **same embedding model** for your documents and for search queries. Vectors from different models can't be compared.
- Inputs longer than the model's context are truncated by default. Split long documents into chunks first.

A simple semantic search: embed all document chunks once and store the vectors (in a list, or a vector database for larger sets). For a question, embed it, compute similarity with each stored vector and take the best matches. That is the retrieval half of RAG; frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex can do it with Ollama embeddings too.

Embedding models are small and fast, so they often run comfortably on a CPU.
concepts.code:
import ollama

docs = ["Refunds are processed within 5 business days.",
        "Our office is closed on public holidays.",
        "You can reset your password from the login page."]
doc_vecs = ollama.embed(model="embeddinggemma", input=docs).embeddings
print(len(doc_vecs), len(doc_vecs[0]))            # 3 768

def similarity(a, b):                             # vectors are normalised: dot = cosine
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))

question = "How long until I get my money back?"
q_vec = ollama.embed(model="embeddinggemma", input=question).embeddings[0]

scores = [similarity(q_vec, v) for v in doc_vecs]
best = max(range(len(docs)), key=lambda i: scores[i])
print(round(scores[best], 2), docs[best])         # 0.62 Refunds are processed within 5 business days.
takeaways: `ollama.embed(model, input=[...])` returns one vector per input
Vectors are normalised: dot product = cosine similarity
Use the same embedding model for documents and queries; chunk long texts
pitfalls: Embedding documents with one model and queries with another, which makes similarity scores meaningless.

quiz.q: Why send a list of 100 chunks in one embed call instead of 100 separate calls?
options: Batching is much faster and reduces request overhead
quiz.explain: One batched request avoids per-request overhead and lets the server process inputs together.

concepts.name: Structured outputs with JSON schemas
concepts.summary: Force a model's reply to match a JSON schema with the format parameter, using Pydantic models to define and validate it.
concepts.why: Programs need reliable fields, and schema-constrained output makes even small local models dependable for extraction.
concepts.body:
Asking "reply in JSON" in the prompt works most of the time. For code that depends on the result, *most of the time* isn't enough. Ollama can **constrain** the output to a JSON schema (a description of the fields and their types), so the reply always parses.

Pass the schema in the `format` parameter. In Python, the easy way to write a schema is **Pydantic**, a library where you describe data as a class: a named template listing fields and their types. Pydantic converts it to a JSON schema and later checks the reply:

```python
class Country(BaseModel):
    name: str
    capital: str
    languages: list[str]

response = chat(model="gpt-oss", messages=[...], format=Country.model_json_schema())
country = Country.model_validate_json(response.message.content)
```

`country.capital` is now a real field you can use.

Tips from the docs and practice:

- Set `temperature` to 0 for consistent extraction.
- Also describe the expected fields in the prompt; it helps the model fill them with the right content.
- `format="json"` only guarantees valid JSON of any shape; a schema is stricter.
- The schema guarantees *shape*, not *truth*: values can still be wrong or invented. Validate important values in code and allow empty or optional fields when data may be missing.
- Over the REST API, put the schema object in the `"format"` field. The OpenAI-compatible API supports structured output through `response_format`.

Structured outputs are a local feature; the docs note Ollama's cloud does not support them.
concepts.code:
from typing import Literal, Optional
from ollama import chat
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Ticket(BaseModel):
    category: Literal["billing", "bug", "other"]
    urgency: int                       # 1 (low) to 5 (critical)
    order_id: Optional[str] = None     # None if not mentioned

text = "I was charged twice for order A-1042, please fix this today!"
response = chat(
    model="gpt-oss",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
               f"Extract category, urgency (1-5) and order_id from: {text}"}],
    format=Ticket.model_json_schema(),  # constrain the reply to this schema
    options={"temperature": 0},
)
ticket = Ticket.model_validate_json(response.message.content)
print(ticket)                          # category='billing' urgency=5 order_id='A-1042'
print(ticket.order_id)                 # A-1042
takeaways: `format=Model.model_json_schema()` constrains output to a schema
`Model.model_validate_json(...)` parses and checks the reply
Schemas guarantee shape, not correctness; use temperature 0 and validate values
pitfalls: Trusting a schema-valid reply as correct, when the model may still have invented a value such as an order ID.

quiz.q: What does passing a JSON schema in format guarantee?
options: That the reply follows the schema's structure and types
quiz.explain: Constrained decoding enforces structure; the content can still be wrong.

concepts.name: Tool calling with local models
concepts.summary: Let a local model call your Python functions: pass tools, run the requested calls, send results back, and loop.
concepts.why: Tool calling turns a local model into an agent that can look things up and act, all on your own machine.
concepts.body:
With tool calling, the model can ask your program to run a function, for example to look up the weather or query a database. The model never runs code itself: it replies with a request, your code runs it, and you send the result back.

With the Python library you can pass ordinary functions as tools. Their names, parameter types and docstrings are turned into descriptions for the model, so write clear docstrings:

```python
def get_temperature(city: str) -> str:
    """Get the current temperature for a city."""
```

The loop:

1. Call `chat(model, messages, tools=[get_temperature])`.
2. If `response.message.tool_calls` is set, each call has `call.function.name` and `call.function.arguments` (a dictionary).
3. Add the assistant message to `messages`, run each requested function, and add a message `{"role": "tool", "tool_name": name, "content": result}` for each.
4. Call `chat` again with the longer history. Repeat until the reply has no tool calls; that reply is the answer.

Models may request several tools at once, or one after another. Use a model with the **tools** capability (shown by `ollama show`); the docs' examples use `qwen3` with thinking enabled.

Practical advice:

- Keep the tool list short and the descriptions specific.
- Check arguments before acting; small models sometimes pass wrong types or invent values.
- Never let a tool do something irreversible (payments, deletions, emails) without confirmation.
- Put a maximum number of rounds on the loop.

Frameworks such as LangChain, LlamaIndex or CrewAI can run this loop for you on Ollama models.
takeaways: Pass Python functions as `tools=`; docstrings become descriptions
Run each `tool_calls` entry and reply with `role: tool` messages
Loop until no tool calls, with a maximum number of rounds
pitfalls: Running whatever function name the model returns without checking it exists and that its arguments are valid.

quiz.q: After the model returns tool_calls, what must your code send in the next chat request?
options: The assistant message plus a tool message with each function's result
quiz.explain: The model needs its own request and the results to continue; tool messages carry the results.

concepts.name: Thinking and vision models
concepts.summary: Enable and control reasoning output with think, and send images to vision-capable models.
concepts.why: Reasoning and image understanding open up harder tasks, but they change speed, cost and how you read responses.
concepts.body:
**Thinking models** can reason step by step before answering, which helps with maths, logic and planning. Ollama separates the reasoning from the final answer:

- In the Python library and REST API, set `think=True`. The reasoning arrives in `message.thinking` and the answer in `message.content`.
- Some models accept named levels instead of true/false, such as `think="low"`, `"medium"` or `"high"` for gpt-oss. The model's details (`/api/show`) list which values it supports; others only support on or off.
- In the terminal: `ollama run MODEL --think`, or `--hidethinking` to keep the reasoning out of the output. In a chat, `/set think` and `/set nothink` toggle it.

Thinking costs time: the model may write hundreds of reasoning tokens before the answer starts. Use it when quality matters more than speed, and switch it off for simple tasks. When streaming, thinking chunks come first; show them separately or hide them. Don't treat the reasoning text as a reliable explanation of how the answer was produced.

**Vision models** understand images: describe photos, read screenshots, extract text from receipts. Check for the **vision** capability with `ollama show`. Send images:

- In the terminal: put the image file path in the prompt.
- In Python: `{"role": "user", "content": "What is in this picture?", "images": ["photo.jpg"]}`. Paths, raw bytes or base64 strings are accepted.
- In the REST API: base64-encoded strings in the message's `images` list.

Images use many tokens, so they need more context and memory. Vision can be combined with structured outputs, for example to extract receipt fields into a schema.
concepts.code:
from ollama import chat

# Thinking: reasoning and answer arrive in separate fields
r = chat(model="qwen3",
         messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. "
                    "The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much is the ball?"}],
         think=True)
print("THINKING:", r.message.thinking[:80], "...")
print("ANSWER:", r.message.content)          # The ball costs $0.05.

# Some models take a level instead of True/False
r2 = chat(model="gpt-oss", think="low",
          messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Is 221 a prime number?"}])

# Vision: attach images to a user message
v = chat(model="gemma4", messages=[{
    "role": "user",
    "content": "List the items and the total on this receipt.",
    "images": ["receipt.jpg"],                # file path, bytes or base64
}])
print(v.message.content)
takeaways: `think=True` (or a level) puts reasoning in `message.thinking`
Thinking improves hard tasks but adds latency; turn it off for simple ones
Vision models take images via `images` in a user message
pitfalls: Displaying the thinking field to end users as the answer, or parsing it as if it were the final output.

quiz.q: With think=True, where is the final answer in the Python library's response?
quiz.explain: Reasoning goes to message.thinking; the answer itself stays in message.content.

concepts.name: Ollama in LangChain, LlamaIndex and n8n
concepts.summary: Use Ollama models from LangChain, LlamaIndex and n8n, and know the settings that commonly trip people up.
concepts.why: Most real apps use Ollama through a framework or automation tool rather than raw API calls.
concepts.body:
Popular frameworks have Ollama integrations, so swapping a hosted model for a local one is often a few lines.

**LangChain** (package `langchain-ollama`):

- `ChatOllama(model="qwen3:8b", temperature=0)` is a chat model with the usual LangChain interface (`invoke`, `stream`, tools, structured output).
- `OllamaEmbeddings(model="embeddinggemma")` for embeddings.
- Useful arguments: `num_ctx` for context length, `reasoning=True` for thinking models, `base_url` for a remote server.

**LlamaIndex** (packages `llama-index-llms-ollama` and `llama-index-embeddings-ollama`):

- `Ollama(model="qwen3:8b", request_timeout=120.0, context_window=16000)`. Raise `request_timeout` (30 seconds by default), because local models on modest hardware can be slow, especially the first call while the model loads.
- `OllamaEmbedding(model_name="embeddinggemma")`.

**n8n** (a no-code automation tool): create an **Ollama** credential with the base URL `http://localhost:11434`. If n8n runs in Docker, `localhost` means the container itself, so use `http://host.docker.internal:11434` instead (on Linux servers, add a host mapping for that name). Then pick an Ollama model in the chat model or embeddings nodes.

Many other tools (coding assistants, chat interfaces, CrewAI and more) connect the same way: a base URL plus a model name, or the OpenAI-compatible `/v1` endpoint.

Common problems: the model isn't downloaded (pull it first), the context is too small for agents and RAG prompts, timeouts on the first slow call, and wrong addresses between containers.
concepts.code:
# pip install langchain-ollama llama-index-llms-ollama llama-index-embeddings-ollama
from langchain_ollama import ChatOllama, OllamaEmbeddings

llm = ChatOllama(model="qwen3:8b", temperature=0, num_ctx=16384)
print(llm.invoke("Give one tip for naming variables.").content)
vec = OllamaEmbeddings(model="embeddinggemma").embed_query("hello")
print(len(vec))                                   # 768

from llama_index.core import Settings
from llama_index.embeddings.ollama import OllamaEmbedding
from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama

Settings.llm = Ollama(model="qwen3:8b", request_timeout=120.0, context_window=16000)
Settings.embed_model = OllamaEmbedding(model_name="embeddinggemma")
print(Settings.llm.complete("Say hi in 3 words.").text)

# n8n in Docker -> Ollama credential base URL: http://host.docker.internal:11434
takeaways: LangChain: `ChatOllama` and `OllamaEmbeddings` (langchain-ollama)
LlamaIndex: `Ollama` (raise request_timeout) and `OllamaEmbedding`
Apps in Docker reach the host's Ollama via host.docker.internal
pitfalls: Using http://localhost:11434 from a container, which points at the container itself rather than the host running Ollama.

quiz.q: n8n runs in Docker and Ollama runs on the same computer outside Docker. Which base URL should the n8n credential use?
quiz.explain: Inside a container, localhost is the container; host.docker.internal reaches the host machine.

concepts.name: Performance: GPU use, keep-alive and concurrency
concepts.summary: Tune speed and memory with GPU checks, keep_alive, parallel requests, loaded-model limits, flash attention and KV-cache quantization.
concepts.why: The same model can be fast or painfully slow depending on a handful of settings.
concepts.body:
**1. Keep the model on the GPU.** Check `ollama ps`. Anything other than `100% GPU` (or full use of Apple unified memory) usually means a big slowdown. Fixes: a smaller model, a lower quantization, or a smaller context.

**2. Avoid reloading.** Loading a model takes seconds. After a request, Ollama keeps the model loaded for 5 minutes by default. Change this per request with `keep_alive` (`"30m"`, `-1` for "keep forever", `0` for "unload now") or for the server with `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE`. To preload a model before users arrive, send a request with no prompt, or run `ollama run MODEL ""`.

**3. Concurrency.** These server settings (environment variables) control many simultaneous requests:

- `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` (default 1): requests one model handles at the same time. Higher values need more memory, because each parallel slot needs its own context.
- `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS`: how many different models may be loaded together (default 3 per GPU, or 3 on CPU).
- `OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE` (default 512): waiting requests before the server answers "busy" (HTTP 503).

**4. Memory-saving features.** Flash attention, a faster and more memory-efficient way of doing one of the model's core calculations, is used automatically when supported (`OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION` forces it on or off). The **KV cache**, the memory that holds the context while generating, can be quantized with `OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0`, which roughly halves its memory with little quality loss; `q4_0` saves more but hurts quality more.

**5. Measure.** `ollama run MODEL --verbose` and the API's `eval_count` and `eval_duration` fields give tokens per second. Compare settings on the same prompt.
concepts.code:
# Load once and keep the model in memory for an hour
curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{"model": "qwen3:8b", "keep_alive": "1h"}'

# Unload now
curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{"model": "qwen3:8b", "keep_alive": 0}'

# Server tuning (Linux shell; restart the server afterwards)
OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4 \
OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=2 \
OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0 \
OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=30m \
ollama serve

# Measure speed
ollama run qwen3:8b --verbose "Explain DNS in two sentences."
# ... eval rate: 61.2 tokens/s
ollama ps    # PROCESSOR should say 100% GPU
takeaways: Check `ollama ps`: aim for 100% GPU
`keep_alive` / `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE` avoid reload delays; empty request preloads
NUM_PARALLEL, MAX_LOADED_MODELS, MAX_QUEUE and KV-cache type trade memory for throughput
pitfalls: Raising OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL on a GPU that is already full, which pushes the model partly onto the CPU and makes every request slower.

quiz.q: Users complain the first request after a quiet period takes 10 seconds, later ones are fast. What helps?
options: Increase keep_alive (or preload the model) so it stays in memory
quiz.explain: The delay is model loading after it was unloaded; a longer keep-alive keeps it ready.

concepts.name: Configuring the Ollama server
concepts.summary: Set server environment variables on macOS, Linux and Windows, move model storage, and read logs.
concepts.why: Real setups need models on a bigger disk, remote access or tuned limits, all controlled by server settings.
concepts.body:
The Ollama server reads its settings from **environment variables** (named values the operating system passes to programs). `ollama serve --help` lists them. Common ones:

- `OLLAMA_HOST`: the address and port to listen on. Default `127.0.0.1:11434`, which only accepts connections from the same computer.
- `OLLAMA_MODELS`: the folder where models are stored, for example a larger disk.
- `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE`, `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH`, `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL`: defaults covered in other lessons.
- `OLLAMA_ORIGINS`: extra web origins (sites or browser extensions) allowed to call the API from a browser.
- `OLLAMA_DEBUG=1`: more detailed logs.
- `OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1`: turn off cloud features.

**Setting them depends on the system:**

- **macOS (app)**: `launchctl setenv OLLAMA_MODELS /Volumes/Big/models` for each variable, then quit and restart the Ollama app.
- **Linux (systemd service)**: run `sudo systemctl edit ollama.service`, add lines like `Environment="OLLAMA_MODELS=/data/ollama"` under `[Service]`, then `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo systemctl restart ollama`. The `ollama` system user needs read and write access to a new models folder.
- **Windows**: quit Ollama, add the variables in your account's environment variables settings, then start Ollama again.

Setting a variable in your own terminal doesn't affect a server that the app or service already started; this is the most common confusion.

**Logs:** on Linux, `journalctl -e -u ollama`. On macOS, `~/.ollama/logs/server.log`. On Windows, the logs folder under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Ollama`. Logs show GPU detection, memory estimates and load errors.

**Proxies:** if downloads must go through a company proxy, set `HTTPS_PROXY` for the server.
concepts.code:
# Linux (systemd): move models and allow network access
sudo systemctl edit ollama.service
#   [Service]
#   Environment="OLLAMA_MODELS=/data/ollama/models"
#   Environment="OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434"
sudo mkdir -p /data/ollama/models && sudo chown -R ollama:ollama /data/ollama
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart ollama
journalctl -e -u ollama            # check startup, GPU detection, errors

# macOS (app): set, then restart the Ollama app
launchctl setenv OLLAMA_MODELS "/Volumes/Big/ollama-models"

# Any OS: list supported variables
ollama serve --help
takeaways: Server settings are environment variables (`ollama serve --help`)
Set them via launchctl (macOS), systemd override (Linux) or system settings (Windows), then restart
Logs: journalctl on Linux, ~/.ollama/logs on macOS
pitfalls: Exporting a variable in a terminal and expecting the already-running app or service to pick it up.

quiz.q: On Linux you set OLLAMA_MODELS in your shell profile, but the service still uses the old folder. Why?
options: The systemd service doesn't read your shell profile; set it in the service override and restart
quiz.explain: Services get their environment from systemd configuration, not from a user's shell.

concepts.name: Running Ollama in Docker
concepts.summary: Run the official ollama/ollama image with persistent model storage and NVIDIA or AMD GPU access.
concepts.why: Containers make Ollama easy to deploy on servers and alongside other services.
concepts.body:
Docker runs programs in **containers**: isolated packages with everything the program needs. Ollama publishes an official image, `ollama/ollama`.

**CPU only:**

```bash
docker run -d -v ollama:/root/.ollama -p 11434:11434 --name ollama ollama/ollama
```

- `-d` runs it in the background.
- `-v ollama:/root/.ollama` stores models in a Docker **volume** named `ollama`, so they survive when the container is replaced. Without it, every new container downloads models again.
- `-p 11434:11434` makes the API reachable on the host's port 11434.

**NVIDIA GPUs:** install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on the host, configure Docker to use it, then add `--gpus=all`.

**AMD GPUs:** use the `ollama/ollama:rocm` image and pass the devices with `--device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri`. The standard image also includes Vulkan support, used when the container can access GPU devices.

Run commands inside the container with `docker exec`:

```bash
docker exec -it ollama ollama run llama3.2
```

**Docker Compose** files work the same way: an `ollama` service with the volume, the port and GPU reservations. Other containers in the same Compose project reach it at `http://ollama:11434`, using the service name instead of `localhost`.

Pass settings as environment variables with `-e`, for example `-e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=1h`.

Publishing the port with `-p 11434:11434` exposes the API on all of the host's network interfaces by default. On a shared network or server, bind it to localhost (`-p 127.0.0.1:11434:11434`) or protect it; the security lesson explains why.
concepts.code:
# NVIDIA GPU, persistent models, API only on this machine
docker run -d --gpus=all \
  -v ollama:/root/.ollama \
  -p 127.0.0.1:11434:11434 \
  -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=1h \
  --name ollama ollama/ollama

docker exec -it ollama ollama pull qwen3:8b
docker exec -it ollama ollama ps

# docker-compose.yml (excerpt)
# services:
#   ollama:
#     image: ollama/ollama
#     volumes: ["ollama:/root/.ollama"]
#     deploy:
#       resources:
#         reservations:
#           devices: [{driver: nvidia, count: all, capabilities: [gpu]}]
#   app:
#     environment: ["OLLAMA_HOST=http://ollama:11434"]   # service name, not localhost
# volumes: {ollama: {}}
takeaways: `ollama/ollama` image; `-v ollama:/root/.ollama` keeps models
`--gpus=all` (NVIDIA) or the `:rocm` image with devices (AMD)
Other containers use the service name, e.g. http://ollama:11434
pitfalls: Forgetting the volume, so every container update re-downloads many gigabytes of models.

quiz.q: Why mount a volume at /root/.ollama when running the Ollama container?
options: So downloaded models persist across container restarts and upgrades
It is required for the CLI
quiz.explain: Models live in /root/.ollama; a volume keeps them when the container is recreated.

concepts.name: Ollama cloud models
concepts.summary: Use Ollama's hosted cloud models from the app, CLI and API, and understand the privacy and feature trade-offs.
concepts.why: Cloud models let you use models too large for your hardware without changing your tools, but data leaves your machine.
concepts.body:
Some open models are far too large for a laptop. **Ollama cloud models** run them on Ollama's servers, while you keep using the same app, CLI and API.

**From the app or CLI:** sign in with `ollama signin` (or the app's setup prompts), then run a cloud model by its `:cloud` name, for example `ollama run gemma4:cloud`. Your local Ollama forwards the request to the cloud. The model list at ollama.com (filter by cloud) shows what is available.

**From code, directly:** create an API key in your ollama.com account settings and set it as the `OLLAMA_API_KEY` environment variable. Then call `https://ollama.com/api/chat` with the header `Authorization: Bearer <key>`, or use `https://ollama.com/v1` with OpenAI-compatible clients. With the API, use the model's full name from the list (such as `gemma4:31b`). In Python, `Client(host="https://ollama.com", headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + key})` works with the same methods.

**Trade-offs:**

- Data leaves your machine. Ollama states that cloud prompts and responses are only used to serve your requests and not for training; still check whether that meets your requirements.
- Usage is metered per account, and models can be retired; your account page shows usage and upcoming retirements. Check current plans on ollama.com rather than relying on remembered prices.
- Some features differ: for example, the docs say structured outputs aren't supported in the cloud, and stateful parts of the Responses API aren't available.

To guarantee nothing goes to the cloud (for example on company laptops), disable cloud features with `OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1` or `"disable_ollama_cloud": true` in `~/.ollama/server.json`.
concepts.code:
# CLI: sign in once, then use ":cloud" model names
ollama signin
ollama run gemma4:cloud "Explain vector databases in two sentences."

# API: call the cloud directly with an API key from ollama.com
export OLLAMA_API_KEY="..."
curl https://ollama.com/api/chat \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OLLAMA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{"model": "gemma4:31b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}], "stream": false}'

# Python (same library, different host)
# from ollama import Client
# client = Client(host="https://ollama.com",
#                 headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["OLLAMA_API_KEY"]})

# Company laptops: keep everything local
OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 ollama serve
takeaways: `ollama signin` + `:cloud` names in the app/CLI
Direct API: https://ollama.com with `OLLAMA_API_KEY` as a bearer token
Data leaves your machine; some features differ; `OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1` disables it
pitfalls: Assuming every local feature works the same in the cloud, such as schema-constrained structured outputs.

quiz.q: An organisation must ensure Ollama never sends prompts off the laptop. What should it configure?
quiz.explain: Disabling cloud features removes cloud models and web search so everything stays local.

concepts.name: Securing an exposed Ollama server
concepts.summary: Expose Ollama safely: understand that the API has no authentication, and add network limits, a reverse proxy and model hygiene.
concepts.why: Many Ollama servers have been found openly reachable on the internet; an exposed API invites abuse and data leaks.
concepts.body:
By default Ollama listens only on `127.0.0.1`, so nothing outside your computer can reach it. That changes when you set `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0` (listen on all network interfaces) or publish a Docker port.

**The local API has no login.** Anyone who can reach the port can:

- run models on your hardware, using your GPU and electricity,
- pull, create and **delete** models,
- see which models you have and probe for weaknesses in the server.

So never expose port 11434 directly to the internet. Instead:

- **Firewall**: allow only the machines that need access, such as your app servers or computers on your company's private network.
- **Reverse proxy with authentication**: put a web server such as Nginx or Caddy in front. It checks an API key or login and uses HTTPS, then forwards allowed requests to Ollama on localhost. Allow only the endpoints your app needs (for example `/api/chat` and `/api/embed`) and block model management (`/api/pull`, `/api/create`, `/api/delete`, `/api/push`).
- **Private networking**: in Docker, publish to `127.0.0.1` or keep Ollama on an internal network reachable only by your app containers.
- **Rate limits** at the proxy, so one client can't monopolise the GPU.
- **Browser access**: `OLLAMA_ORIGINS` controls which websites may call the API from a browser; keep it as narrow as possible.

**Model hygiene:** pull models from sources you trust, pin tags, keep Ollama updated (security fixes ship in releases) and review a model's Modelfile, since a malicious `SYSTEM` prompt can steer behaviour.

Finally, the usual LLM risks still apply to what you build on top: prompt injection through documents, and tools that act without checks.
takeaways: The Ollama API has no built-in authentication; anyone who reaches it has full control
Keep it on localhost or a private network; add a reverse proxy with auth and HTTPS
Block model-management endpoints and rate-limit at the proxy
pitfalls: Setting OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 on a cloud VM with an open firewall, letting anyone on the internet use and delete your models.

quiz.q: You need a web app on another server to use your Ollama box. What is the safest setup?
options: Set OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 and open port 11434 to the internet
Share the server's password with the app
Keep Ollama on localhost behind a reverse proxy that requires an API key, uses HTTPS and allows only needed endpoints
quiz.explain: Since Ollama has no authentication, a proxy must enforce access control and limit endpoints.

concepts.name: Importing, quantizing and sharing models
concepts.summary: Import GGUF or Safetensors weights (including fine-tunes) with a Modelfile, quantize Safetensors imports, and push models to ollama.com.
concepts.why: Fine-tuned and niche models often aren't in the library; importing lets you run them like any other model.
concepts.body:
Not every model is in the Ollama library. You may have fine-tuned one yourself or found it on Hugging Face (a large public hub for models). Ollama can import two common file formats:

- **GGUF**: a single-file format from the llama.cpp project, usually already quantized (file names contain things like `Q4_K_M`).
- **Safetensors**: the standard format for original, unquantized weights, typically a folder with several files plus configuration.

**Import** with a Modelfile whose `FROM` points at the files:

```
FROM ./my-model-Q4_K_M.gguf
```

or `FROM /path/to/safetensors/folder`, then run `ollama create my-model`. Split GGUF files keep their original names and can be referenced with a wildcard such as `FROM ./model-*.gguf`.

**Quantization during import:** for Safetensors imports, `ollama create my-model --quantize int4` (short `-q`) creates a smaller quantized version. Current versions accept levels such as `int4`, `int8`, `nvfp4`, `mxfp4` and `mxfp8`; an unsupported value prints the list for your version. GGUF files are not re-quantized; quantize them beforehand with llama.cpp's tools.

**Prompt template:** chat models are trained with a specific format for roles. Ollama detects common ones automatically. If an imported model gives strange, rambling answers, the template is likely wrong; copy the `TEMPLATE` from a library model of the same family (`ollama show family --modelfile`).

**Sharing:** create an account on ollama.com, add your Ollama public key in its settings, name the model with your username (`ollama cp my-model myuser/my-model`), then `ollama push myuser/my-model`. Others run it with `ollama run myuser/my-model`.

Respect licenses: many open-weight models restrict commercial use or redistribution.
concepts.code:
# 1) Import a GGUF file (already quantized)
cat > Modelfile <<'EOF'
FROM ./support-bot-Q4_K_M.gguf
PARAMETER temperature 0.3
SYSTEM You are Acme's support assistant.
EOF
ollama create support-bot -f Modelfile
ollama run support-bot "Where is my order?"

# 2) Import Safetensors weights and quantize while importing
echo "FROM ./my-finetune-safetensors" > Modelfile.st
ollama create --help                       # check supported --quantize levels
ollama create my-finetune -f Modelfile.st --quantize int4

# 3) Share on ollama.com (after adding your public key in account settings)
ollama cp support-bot myuser/support-bot
ollama push myuser/support-bot
takeaways: `FROM ./file.gguf` or `FROM ./safetensors-folder`, then `ollama create`
`--quantize` works for Safetensors imports; GGUF must be quantized beforehand
Wrong TEMPLATE causes odd answers; `ollama push user/model` shares it
pitfalls: Importing a chat fine-tune whose prompt template Ollama doesn't recognise and blaming the fine-tune for gibberish answers.

quiz.q: You have an unquantized Safetensors fine-tune that is too big for your GPU. What can Ollama do at import time?
options: Convert it to a cloud model
quiz.explain: Create-time quantization is supported for Safetensors imports (not for GGUF).

concepts.name: Serving many users with Ollama
concepts.summary: Plan capacity, concurrency, model versioning and monitoring for a shared Ollama service, and know when to use another engine.
concepts.why: A tool that is great on one laptop needs deliberate planning to serve a team or an application reliably.
concepts.body:
Ollama can serve a small team or an internal app well. Doing it reliably takes some planning.

**Capacity.** Throughput depends on GPU memory and speed. Memory is roughly: model weights + (parallel slots × context length × per-token KV-cache cost). Test with realistic prompts: measure tokens per second and time to the first token while sending several requests at once, then pick `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` and the context length that keep everything on the GPU. Requests beyond the parallel limit wait in a queue (`OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE`); clients should handle HTTP 503 "busy" replies by retrying later.

**Keep models warm.** Set `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE` to keep production models loaded, limit `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS`, and avoid letting users switch between many models on one GPU; every switch means a slow reload.

**Scale out.** For more users, run several Ollama servers (each with its own GPU) behind a load balancer, a component that spreads incoming requests across them. Keep them identical: the same Ollama version, the same pinned model tags, and the same custom Modelfiles from version control. Treat a model update like a code release: test, then roll out.

**Monitor.** Log request counts, queue waits, errors, tokens per second and GPU memory (for example with `nvidia-smi` and the server logs). Check `ollama ps` for CPU spills after changes.

**Know the limits.** Ollama focuses on simplicity. For very high concurrency on large GPU servers, dedicated serving engines (such as vLLM or other high-throughput servers) usually serve more requests per GPU, at the cost of more setup. Many teams prototype on Ollama and move only their busiest models.

Security from the previous lesson applies: authentication and rate limits at a proxy in front of every server.
concepts.code:
# Simple load test: N concurrent chats, report latency and tokens/s
import concurrent.futures, time
from ollama import Client

client = Client(host="http://127.0.0.1:11434")
PROMPT = [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a 3-sentence product description for a desk lamp."}]

def one_call(_):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    r = client.chat(model="qwen3:8b", messages=PROMPT, options={"num_predict": 120})
    return time.perf_counter() - start, r.eval_count / (r.eval_duration / 1e9)

for workers in (1, 4, 8):
    with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers) as pool:
        results = list(pool.map(one_call, range(workers * 2)))
    lat = sorted(r[0] for r in results)
    tps = sum(r[1] for r in results) / len(results)
    print(f"{workers} parallel: median {lat[len(lat)//2]:.1f}s, {tps:.0f} tok/s per request")
# 1 parallel: median 2.1s, 62 tok/s ... compare against OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL settings
takeaways: Size memory for weights + parallel slots × context; keep it all on the GPU
Pin versions and model tags; scale out with identical servers behind a load balancer
Monitor queueing and speed; consider dedicated engines for very high concurrency
pitfalls: Letting every user pick any model on a shared GPU server, causing constant model reloads and long waits for everyone.

quiz.q: Clients get HTTP 503 responses from Ollama during peak hours. What does that indicate?
options: The request queue is full; capacity or parallel settings are insufficient for the load
The context length is too large
quiz.explain: 503 means the server is too busy (queue limit reached); add capacity or tune concurrency.
